title: Measuring a cart's acceleration down a ramp

stimulus.title: Release distance and time on a ramp
stimulus.html:
A group wants to find the acceleration of a cart rolling down a long, straight ramp, which they expect to be constant. They have a cart, the ramp, a meterstick and a stopwatch, and they may use a photogate. In part (c) you will use their data below: for each release distance d, measured along the ramp from the release point to a photogate at the bottom, they released the cart from rest three times and recorded the time t to reach the photogate.

Time for the cart to roll a distance d from rest (three trials)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe a procedure the group could use to collect data from which the cart's acceleration can be found. Name each quantity measured and the instrument used to measure it, and include a way to reduce experimental uncertainty.

rubric.point: Release the cart from rest and measure the distance d along the ramp with the meterstick
accept: measures distance traveled along the ramp with a meterstick or tape measure

rubric.point: Measure the time t to travel that distance with the stopwatch or a photogate
accept: times the run with a stopwatch, or a photogate at the end point

rubric.point: Reduces uncertainty: repeats each distance several times and averages, and/or uses a range of at least five different distances

parts.sample: Mark a finish point near the bottom of the ramp and place a photogate there. Use the meterstick to measure a release distance d along the ramp from the finish, and release the cart from rest at that mark (let go without pushing). Record the time t from release to the finish: start a stopwatch as you let go and stop it as the cart reaches the mark, or use a photogate timer started at release and stopped at the finish. Repeat three times for each distance and average the times. Do this for five distances, from 0.20 m to 1.00 m.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Indicate what quantities the group should plot to produce a linear graph, and explain how the acceleration of the cart can be found from that graph.

rubric.point: Plot d against t² (or t² against d), justified by d = ½at² for a start from rest
accept: d on the vertical axis, t² on the horizontal axis
a straight line through the origin because d ∝ t²

rubric.point: States the slope of d against t² is ½a, so a = 2 × slope (or for t² against d, slope = 2/a, so a = 2/slope)

parts.sample: For a cart starting from rest with constant acceleration, d = ½at². Plot d on the vertical axis against t² on the horizontal axis. This is a straight line through the origin, y = mx with y = d and x = t², whose slope m = ½a. So a = 2 × slope.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Plot the data on the axes provided, using the quantities from part (b). Label the axes with quantities and units, use a linear scale, and draw a best-fit line.

rubric.point: Both axes labeled with the plotted quantity and a unit (d in m, t² in s²)
accept: labels and units on both axes

rubric.point: Five correctly calculated and plotted points on linear scales that use most of the grid
accept: points plotted within half a grid square

rubric.point: A single straight best-fit line through the data, with points on both sides, not connecting the dots
accept: one straight line, roughly through the origin

parts.sample: Horizontal axis "t² (s²)" from 0 to 2.5 in steps of 0.5; vertical axis "d (m)" from 0 to 1.2 in steps of 0.2. Points: (0.49, 0.20), (0.94, 0.40), (1.46, 0.60), (1.88, 0.80), (2.40, 1.00). One straight ruled line through the points and close to the origin, with points scattered on both sides of it.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate the acceleration of the cart using the best-fit line from part (c).

rubric.point: Slope found from two points on the best-fit line (not two data points unless they lie on the line), with units of m/s²
a = 2 × slope ≈ 0.84 m/s² with units (0.76 to 0.90 m/s² accepted)
accept: acceleration twice the slope, in m/s²

parts.sample: Two points on my line: (0.00 s², 0.00 m) and (2.40 s², 1.00 m). Slope = 1.00 m ÷ 2.40 s² = 0.417 m/s². Since the slope is ½a, a = 2 × 0.417 m/s² = 0.83 m/s² (a least-squares fit gives 0.84 m/s²; any value from a reasonable line earns the point).
